ending: two consecutive rounds with no confirmed blocking or misleading finding, both gates green, frozen surface, self-inflicted under 25%

rounds.headline: Seven blind seats, none signing off. Five misleading findings, all in the degraded states or the headline: the quiet state reassured over three marks that contradicted it, first-run held a six-week-old job in a three-day-old account, the hero folded the running week into a comparison against four whole ones, the error state stamped a successful read at the instant of the failure, and marks at 390 stole each other's hit boxes. The most valuable finding was not a defect but a blind gate: the behaviour gate's own open-topped assertion measured the invisible bottom edge and certified the opposite of the contract it guarded.

confirmed.element: .record / .record-tag inside .plot, and @keyframes draw
confirmed.problem: `.record` is a zero-height element (`height: 0`, `border-top: 1px dashed`) carrying `animation: draw ... both`, whose `to` frame sets `clip-path: inset(0 0 0 0)`. A clip-path clips to the element's own border box — here 686×1px — and `.record-tag` is positioned at `top: -18px`, entirely outside it. Measured on the real file at 1440: `.record` computes `clip-path: inset(0px 0% 0px 0px)`, the tag's box is 103×15 at y 433 while the record box is 1px tall at y 450, and a pixel clip of the tag's own rectangle is a blank 206-byte PNG as built versus 1055 bytes with the clip forced off. This holds in settled, in `?motion=play`, on the dark ground, and under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` — the media query's `.record { clip-path: none }` is a normal declaration and is outranked by the animation's filled value, so the author's own escape hatch does not fire. 'Best week · 8' has never rendered, at any width, in any state.
confirmed.consequence: The chart draws a dashed horizontal line across it with no legend anywhere on the visible surface. The reader has to invent a meaning for it, and the obvious guesses — an average, a target — are not what it is. The line is the only thing on the screen that answers 'is this stretch better or worse than my normal', which is half the brief, and sighted readers never get told what it marks. Only the screen-reader sentence carries the fact.
confirmed.fix: Two edits, no reserved gutter. (1) In chart(), emit the tag as a SIBLING of .record inside .plot and give it its own --r: `Best week · ${D.bestPrior}` — the inline --r must be repeated, it is not inherited from a sibling. (2) Replace the .record-tag rule with `position: absolute; left: 0; right: auto; bottom: calc(var(--r) * 1%); margin-bottom: 4px; color: var(--ink-3); background: var(--paper); padding-right: var(--gap-hair);`. Left, not right: the record sits at 8 and every historical column tops out at 7 or below, so the left end of the rule is clear paper while the right end is permanently under the twelfth column, which is the hatched partial bucket and a protected object that must not be knocked out by the label's paper background. Measured with this applied at 390/768/1280/1440: the tag hit-tests as itself at all ten sample points across its width, overlaps zero bars at every breakpoint, column width is unchanged (22 / 43.5 / 53.5 / 53.5), and the x-axis sync is unchanged from baseline. Do NOT add padding-right to .record or .gridline — it is provably inert on a zero-height left:0/right:0 box — and do NOT add it to .cols. If the entrance is still wanted, animate the tag's own opacity on its own delay rather than clipping its parent; and if the draw-in of the rule is to survive at all, either move `clip-path: none` to `!important` in BOTH the [data-motion="settled"] and prefers-reduced-motion blocks (the animation origin outranks a plain author declaration) or, better, move the animated clip off .record onto a `.record::before` carrying the border so nothing that must paint is ever inside a clipped box again.
confirmed.assertion: At 1440 and 390, on both grounds, in settled, in `?motion=play` after the choreography, and in a `reducedMotion: "reduce"` context, screenshot the record tag's bounding box and assert the clip differs from a screenshot of an equal-sized patch of flat card background — i.e. the words actually paint — and assert `getComputedStyle(document.querySelector('.record')).clipPath === 'none'`. Prove the assertion by restoring the clip-path and watching it fail.
confirmed.verdict:
problem affirmed, seat's fix replaced — The OBSERVATION is exactly right and I reproduced every part of it; the finding is refuted on its FIX, which is inert in two of its three edits and destructive in the third. Confirmed first: computed clip-path on .record resolves to inset(0px 0% 0px 0px) at 390/768/1280/1440, on both grounds, under ?motion=settled, ?motion=play after the 1.7s choreography, the webdriver default, and prefers-reduced-motion — the `both` fill of @keyframes draw sits in the animation origin, above the un-!important `[data-motion="settled"] .record { clip-path: none }` and its reduced-motion twin, so the clip is never lifted. .record's border box measures 1px tall (top 450.3, height 1 at 1440); .record-tag measures 433.3-448.1, wholly outside it. elementFromPoint across the tag's own width returns span.cols / span.colw / span.bar at every sample, never the tag. A pixel crop of the tag's rect is byte-identical-free: 871 bytes as shipped versus 2906 bytes with `.record { animation: none !important; clip-path: none !important }` — the crop is blank paper today and carries 'BEST WEEK · 8' with the override. The second-order claim is real too: with the clip lifted the tag paints under the twelfth column, because .cols follows .record in DOM order with no z-index between them, and the hatched partial bar (1227.3-1249.3) lands on the tag's 1162.3-1265 run and eats the '·'. The gates do not cover this — interaction-check.mjs line 520 only compares .record opacity early versus late, and says nothing about the tag reaching the screen. Severity stands: an unlabelled dashed rule across the hero chart reads by convention as a target or threshold, so the sighted owner is invited to conclude 'I am over the line' about a line that is not a target, while the .sr text tells the screen-reader user it is the previous best of 8. The eye gets strictly less than the ear, on the one comparison the movement exists to make.

Why it is nonetheless REFUTED: the proposed `padding-right: 96px` on .plot's .cols, .record and .gridline rules was measured under Playwright and it (a) does nothing at all where the seat says it does, (b) wrecks the chart where it does bite, and (c) carries a wrong number. On .record and .gridline the rules are position:absolute with left:0/right:0/height:0 under the file's global `* { box-sizing: border-box }` — padding cannot shorten a border-top, and both spans measured unchanged before and after (579-1265 at 1440, 41-349 at 390), so the dashed rule and the gridlines still run the full plot width exactly as before. On .cols (inset:0) it does bite, and the cost is severe: column width falls 53.5px to 45.5px at 1440 and 22px to 14px at 390 — a 36% loss of chart on the phone, where the twelve-column composition is a protected object — and every bar shrinks with it at 390 because the bar fills its column there. Worse, .xaxis is a separate flex row in .chart that gets no padding, so the ticks desynchronise from the columns they name: the twelfth column's centre moves 92px away from '13 JUL' at 1440 and 100.8px at 390, which turns a correct axis into a wrong one. And 96px does not even reserve enough — the tag measures 102.7px, so it would still overhang. A fix that leaves the stated target untouched, shrinks the protected phone composition by a third and mislabels the x-axis is worse than the defect it removes.

confirmed.element: .bar-val ("12 so far") against .gridline b ("12") at the top right of the plot
confirmed.problem: The live week's value label and the top gridline's value label overlap on screen at every declared viewport. Measured (light, settled, state=full): at 1440 `.bar-val` is 1204–1272 × 385–400 and the "12" gridline label is 1246–1265 × 392–407 — a 19 × 8px overprint; at 1280 the same; at 768 the same; at 390 `.bar-val` is 304–372 and the label 330–349. The "FAR" of "12 SO FAR" is struck through by a second numeral that happens also to read 12, so two different facts (this week's count and the axis maximum) are drawn on top of each other in the same 11px tracked mono. `.bar-val` also overhangs `.plot`'s right edge by 7px at 1280/1440, 12px at 768 and 23px at 390 — at 390 that carries it past the `.page`'s own 24px right margin. Present in full, partial, quiet and loading, on both grounds; the dark ground is worse because both labels sit on the same #18181b card.
confirmed.consequence: The single most important column on the chart — the week the owner is living in — has its value printed illegibly, over the number that establishes the scale. She either misreads one for the other or, more likely, reads neither and loses both the current count and the chart's magnitude. On a phone the label also breaks the page's right margin, which is the one edge every other element on the surface respects.
confirmed.fix: Do not dodge vertically — the right edge is oversubscribed (axis max, best-week tag, live value) and the answer is to reserve it. Give the plot a right gutter that only the columns are inset from, so the label rail is unoccupied: add `--gutter: 30px` on `.chart`, `.plot .cols { right: var(--gutter); }` and `.xaxis { padding-right: var(--gutter); }`, then right-align the live value with `.colw:last-child .bar-val { left: auto; right: 0; transform: none; }`. I measured this exact stylesheet at all four viewports: the axis label and the bar value separate by 10.8px of clear space at every one (1440: bar-val ends 1235.0, gridline '12' starts 1245.8), bar-val no longer crosses .plot's edge or the page margin at 390, bar and tick centres stay locked at 1440/1280/768, and bars keep their 22px cap. If the `record-tag-never-paints` gutter lands too, use ONE shared --gutter rather than two, and size it to the widest of the three labels ('Best week · 8' measures 102.7px, so the tag must keep right:0 on .record and sit in the gutter, not be inset by it). Leave `.gridline b { top: -14px }` alone — with the gutter it is already clear.
confirmed.assertion: In every state that draws `.bar-val`, at each declared viewport and on both grounds, `.bar-val`'s rect intersects no `.gridline b`, no `.record-tag` and no `.xaxis span`, and `.bar-val.getBoundingClientRect().right <= .plot.getBoundingClientRect().right`.

confirmed.problem: The file resets `box-sizing` and nothing else, so the user-agent stylesheet's `margin: 1em 0` is live on every paragraph and heading. Measured computed margins in state=full: `.t-label` paragraphs 11px top and bottom, `.t-small` 13px, `.t-head` 20px, `.t-sect` 21.58px. The result is that the spacing between typographic blocks is set by the browser, not by the declared ladder. Inside `.limit`, a flex column with `gap: var(--gap-tight)` (8px), the rendered gap from the "Not yet" eyebrow to its heading is 39px and from the heading to its explanation 41px — the authored rung appears nowhere. Same in `.ghost-say` (headline to caption: 37px against an authored 4px), `.stack` (figure to note: 23px against 8px) and `.reading` when it wraps at 390 (49px). Because the UA margin is `1em`, the gap also scales with the font size — the exact coupling the file's own comment rejects for leading ("Leading belongs to a role, not to a size"). The audit gate cannot see this: it reads the SOURCE for raw px in margin, padding and gap, and these numbers are not in the source.
confirmed.consequence: Every relationship the type system expresses through proximity is wrong by three to five times. "Not yet" is meant to be an eyebrow sitting on top of "Open work over time"; at 39px away it reads as an unrelated stamp, and the refusal tiles lose the grouping that makes them scan as three of a kind. The whole surface reads looser and taller than it was drawn — the phone's refusal tiles are 216px tall to hold three short lines — so a reader scrolls further to reach less.

confirmed.element: .kpis — the five cards over the shared denominator, movement two

Make disagreement structurally impossible instead: compute const q = { sitting, overdue, unowned, oldest } from the same accessor the strip reads, and let the quiet band's card be a function of q - reassurance when all three are 0 and every age < D.fortnight, otherwise the count it actually has, still in the quiet band's own layout. Add a second lab-authored set there (e.g. quiet: { jobs, status }) that keeps openCount at the bound activeRootTaskCount of 9 and still carries the three rootTaskTitles verbatim and in order, with all nine ages under 14 and sitting/overdue/unowned/waiting all 0. (3) D must become state-aware, which it is not today: D is built at module scope (~line 466) and D.oldest, D.axisMax, D.sitting, D.overdue, D.unowned and D.peak are all derived there, while the ?state= parse does not run until ~line 830. confirmed.element: .hero-n — the 64px "31", the "+5 on the four before" chip, and the band-head window label
confirmed.problem: The protected partial-bucket treatment is honoured in the chart and abandoned in the headline that dominates the screen. lastFour sums weeks 8–11 (6+8+5+12 = 31) where week 11 is the hatched, open-topped, four-days-old current week, and compares it against four complete weeks (26) as a clean "+5". confirmed.consequence: The delta is the one sentence answering "am I getting on top of this, or just busy?", and it is computed over an incomplete period. On this fixture the partial week happens to run hot, so it flatters; on a Monday morning the same arithmetic prints a large negative and tells an owner they are slipping when in fact the window is one day old. The reader has no way to see which they are looking at, on the single number the whole page is built to deliver.
confirmed.fix: Keep the pill exactly as it is — 189px, one line, unchanged text — and carry the mark on the two lines that already have room. (a) Window label: add one accessor, readingShort, derived from F.bound.readingDate ('2026-07-16' -> '16 Jul') in the same DD Mmm form as w.start, and print 'Last four weeks / 22 Jun to 16 Jul'. Identical character count, zero layout cost, and the ISO date is already bound to src/lib/project-truth-fixture.ts so it cannot drift. While there, derive both bounds from the same constant that produces slice(8) rather than the hardcoded indices 8 and 11, so the label cannot desync from the sum. (b) The partial mark: when D.weeks[D.weeks.length-1].partial is true, extend the existing hero-note from 'jobs finished, Harbour House weddings' to 'jobs finished, Harbour House weddings — this week still running'. confirmed.element: kpi() word strings and the quiet state's sentence
confirmed.problem: The card words are written as plural predicates and pinned to a numeral that can be 1, with no agreement step. On screen the third card reads "1 / have nobody's name on them" and its accessible name reads "1 job have nobody's name on them, of 9 jobs open". confirmed.consequence: Voice is one of the three things this product says are non-negotiable, and the two visible grammar errors are both on the sentences a first-time owner reads most carefully — the one card that names a specific problem and the one line that tells them everything is fine. A screen that cannot conjugate a verb does not read as an instrument, and for the audience this is written for it reads as unfinished software.
confirmed.fix: Change kpi()'s `word` to a pair `{ one, many }` and select with the existing plural() spirit — `const w = n === 1 ? word.one : word.many` — so n = 0 keeps taking the many form, which is already correct today ("0 jobs are waiting on something else"). Use: still — "hasn't moved in a fortnight" / "haven't moved in a fortnight"; nobody — "has nobody's name on it" / "have nobody's name on them"; waiting — "is waiting on something else" / "are waiting on something else". For overdue, do NOT adopt the seat's "are past the day they were due": keep the shipped label byte-identical at "past the day they were due" and pair it with "past the day it was due", so the only string that changes is the one that is currently wrong. Two things the seat's fix leaves unspecified and must be handled: the `unavailable` branch at lately.html:527 builds `${word}: not available…` where the count is unknown by definition — it must take `word.many` explicitly, or it will throw on an object; and the visible label span at line 532 must render the same selected `w` that the .sr name uses, or the card and its accessible name diverge, which is a worse defect than the one being fixed. For the quiet sentence at line 758, do not hard-code "have": build it from the same selection so it agrees at any denominator — "All 9 open jobs have moved inside a fortnight" at n > 1 and "The one open job has moved inside a fortnight" at n = 1, since "All 1 open job have/has moved" is awkward either way. The remainder of that sentence ("none is past its day, and every one has a name on it") is already correct and must not be touched.

confirmed.element: ?state=first-run — the ages strip and KPI row beneath the first-run hero

confirmed.consequence: The state built to make a new owner's first week feel considered instead shows them an account that is six weeks old and already behind. confirmed.fix: Bound first-run by the account's real age, not by 28. Derive accountDays = days between D.weeks[11].iso (2026-07-13) and D.bound.readingDate (2026-07-16) = 3, and build a first-run-scoped slice from it rather than mutating the global D: jobs whose age <= accountDays, axisMax derived from that slice with the Math.max(45, …) floor lifted (it exists to stop a 60-day job falling off its own chart, not to force a 45-day scale onto a three-day account), and the scale marks derived from axisMax instead of the hardcoded [0,15,30,45] list, which degenerates to the single 'today' tick at this range. Recompute all four status counts and the lead denominator from the same slice so the shared-denominator contract still holds — in a three-day-old account 'haven’t moved in a fortnight' is necessarily 0 and the fortnight marker sits past the axis end, so the strip needs a first-run treatment that says nothing has had time to sit rather than drawing a rule nothing can cross. That is a decision, not a filter, which is why the seat's one-line slice does not reach it. If a three-day fixture leaves the band too thin to be worth drawing, the honest alternative is to move the start week back so the account is genuinely a few weeks old and let every figure follow from it — but then '10 August' must move with it, since it is derived from the start week, not typed at random. For the audience this is written for — someone who has never used a tool like this — a promise that does not answer is not a missing feature, it is evidence the screen is broken. Advertising is a promise, and this page checks nobody's.
confirmed.fix: Take the seat's own fallback branch, not its preferred one: delete the second sentence at lately.html:609 so the line reads 'Counted at the moment each job reached a done column.' confirmed.element: State error - "Last good reading . 09:14, Thursday 16 July 2026", against the header's "Read at 09:14, Thursday 16 July 2026" and the coverage strip's "Read 09:14, Thursday 16 July 2026"
confirmed.problem: The reading failed. If a stale reading is ever to be shown it needs its own bound field (a lastGoodReading in derive-fixture.mjs, joined to the bound list, never to labAuthored - a lab-authored staleness stamp would be the same fabrication with a footnote). 2) Do not ship "Nothing has been read today." It swaps one unheld fact for another: the surface has no day-scoped read history either, and "today" is a scope this twelve-week look-back never uses. If a line is wanted where the stamp was, say what is actually known - that the retry is the only way forward - or leave the space empty; the card already carries "Try again". 3) Do not drop the header line alone. The header's "Read at" (725) and the coverage strip's "Read" (735) print the same string under the same verb; removing one and leaving the other keeps the identical claim on screen while breaking the header rule, whose flex rule and "Twelve weeks" chip would be left orphaned (that rule is already fragile at 390 - see reading-rule-dangles-at-390). confirmed.element: .strip-scale - the ticks today / 15d / 30d / 45d under the ages strip
confirmed.problem: The marks are spread by justify-content: space-between, so they land at 0, 33.3, 66.7 and 100 per cent of the strip whatever their values, while every dot is positioned at age / axisMax. The two agree today only because the shipped oldest age, 41, happens to round axisMax to exactly 45. Proven by raising the oldest job to 46: axisMax becomes 50, the ticks stay at 1.9 / 34.7 / 66.8 / 98.9 per cent while 15, 30 and 45 days truly fall at 30, 60 and 90 per cent - the scale detaches from its own marks by up to 100px at 1440.
confirmed.consequence: For any workspace whose oldest open job is not within four days of a multiple of five - most of them - every dot is read against the wrong number, and the reader takes a job that has been sitting three weeks for a job that has been sitting a month. The axis is the only thing on the strip that turns a position into a fact.
confirmed.fix: Two changes, both in the strip. (1) Derive the mark set from the axis instead of hardcoding it: build marks by stepping 15 from 0 while below axisMax and always append axisMax itself, dropping the penultimate mark if it lands within ~8 per cent of the end so the last two labels cannot collide - this guarantees the right-hand end of the axis is always named. (2) Keep `.strip-scale { position: absolute; left:0; right:0; bottom:0 }` exactly as it is, drop `display:flex; justify-content: space-between`, and give it an explicit `height: <the label line-height>` so it does not collapse. Render each mark as `position: absolute; bottom: 0; left: calc(var(--x) * 1%)` with `--x` set to `n / D.axisMax * 100`, the same expression the dots and the fortnight rule already use. For the horizontal anchor do NOT apply a blanket `translateX(-50%)`: give the first mark `transform: none` (left-aligned, as today), the last mark `transform: translateX(-100%)` (right-aligned), and `translateX(-50%)` to every mark between. That reproduces the edge-inset the current space-between gives for free, keeps both end labels inside the strip without a clamp hack, and makes each interior label's centre land on its true value. Re-run both gates afterwards - the scale is a `.t-unit` and moving it changes what backdrop it composites against.

Shipped oldest is 41 (fixture.js), so `D.axisMax = Math.max(45, Math.ceil((41+4)/5)*5) = 45` and the two systems coincide to within 14px at the 15d mark. Forcing the oldest job to 46 via addInitScript: axisMax becomes 50, every dot rescales (the 46-day dot moves to 92 per cent), the ticks do not move at all, and the 45d label sits at 1022.5px where 45 days truly falls at 930.6px - a 92px lie, close to the seat's claimed 100px. confirmed.element: .ghost inside "What this can't tell you"
confirmed.problem: Three refusal tiles sit above one drawn-but-empty plot, and nothing ties the plot to any of them. Its caption — "and it stays empty until the recorder has run for three periods" — names a cause that belongs to exactly one tile ("Open work over time", whose stated reason is that the snapshot writer has no callers). The other two have entirely different, separately named causes: the date recorder only switched on in August, and the third is a Notes change. The plot is presented as the answer to a question the reader has to guess.
confirmed.consequence: The reader cannot tell which refusal they are looking at, and the caption invites the wrong generalisation: that all three of these arrive once the recorder has run. Two of them do not, and one of them is not this product's change at all. The movement's whole value is that the limit is stated where the reader would otherwise assume the opposite, and an unattributed illustration undoes that.
confirmed.fix: Do the tie in visible copy and native semantics; drop the ARIA entirely. (1) Change the ghost's own heading to name its tile: 'Open work over time - the chart we would draw', sub-line unchanged. That is what actually removes the guess, for sighted and screen-reader readers alike. (2) Make the markup say what it is: render .ghost as <figure class="ghost"> with <figcaption class="ghost-say">. figure maps to role figure, which does support a name, and figcaption gives the caption its native relationship to the drawing - no aria-labelledby, no ids threaded through the LIMITS map. (3) If a machine-readable tie is still wanted for the gate, stamp data-limit="open-work-over-time" on the figure and the matching tile rather than inventing an ARIA relationship the role cannot carry. (4) Leave the other two refusals undrawn; one plot answers one refusal, and inventing two more ghosts would turn the movement into a gallery.

confirmed.element: Movement three - the three refusal tiles and the ghost caption in every state

confirmed.element: Refusal tile two - "The date recorder switched on in August." against the reading line "Read at 09:14, Thursday 16 July 2026"

confirmed.element: .reading .rule — the hairline between the reading instant and the window
confirmed.problem: The reading line is a flex row of two label stamps with a `flex: 1 1 40px` hairline between them, so the rule's job is to join the left stamp to the right one. At 390 the row wraps: measured, the date stamp occupies 24–297 at top 192, the rule renders as a 57px stub at 309–366 pointing at nothing, and "TWELVE WEEKS" drops to a second line at top 241 with empty space to its right. The rule survives the wrap as decoration with no function.
confirmed.consequence: A hairline that connects nothing is the kind of stray mark a reader's eye stops on and then has to dismiss, at the top of the screen, before the reading has started. The two stamps also stop reading as one line of context and become two unrelated fragments, which is the opposite of what the reading line is for.
confirmed.fix: Hide the rule across the whole wrap zone and let the two stamps wrap as whole flex items with the separator LEADING the second one, so no mark is ever left at the end of a line. Note the selector must be :not(:first-child) or p ~ p -- `p + p` does not match, because span.rule sits between the two paragraphs. Measured: at 390 this yields line one 24-297 and line two '· Twelve weeks' 24-130, no stray mark, container 106px; at 480 and above (including the 561-580 rail band) it joins into one line, 24-297 plus 305-412, container 61px, identical to today's joined reading. 600px is the threshold because the wrap zone measures 320-476 and 561-580; at 601 the rule returns at ~164px, long enough to read as a connector rather than a stub, so there is no jarring jump at the boundary. This also matches house idiom -- the workspace/owner line and the error state's 'Last good reading · ...' already join with a middot.

confirmed.element: .dot on the ages strip ("How long open work has been sitting"), 390x844 with touch
confirmed.problem: The de-swarm stacks colliding marks on a 15px row pitch, but each mark carries a 34x34 hit expander (.dot::after, inset -11px). A row-1 mark's box therefore covers the row-0 mark's visible disc. Driven with a real touchscreen tap at 390: tapping the exact centre of mark 0 ("Order tonic and the good olives, open 2 days") raises the label for mark 1 ("3 days open · Confirm the Harbour wall cordon with the harbourmaster"), and tapping the centre of mark 2 ("Send the midweek rate to the June 2027 couple, open 5 days") raises mark 3 ("6 days open · Approve the final seating plan"). Only 32% and 43% of those two marks' own hit boxes resolve to themselves. Reproduces identically on full, partial, quiet and first-run. The behaviour gate's closest-pair rule measures euclidean centre distance (16.5px, passes its 12px floor) and is blind to occlusion; audit.mjs measures target size, not who is on top.
confirmed.consequence: On the phone — where the tooltip is the only place a job's title and age appear at all — the owner touches one mark and is told a different job's name and a different number of days. She reads "3 days" off a mark that means 2 days, on the exact object the strip exists to let her interrogate. Two of nine open jobs cannot be inspected at all by pointer, and nothing on screen tells her the reading she got is not the mark she touched.
confirmed.fix: The proposed fix is correct and its arithmetic checks out against the real source - I applied it in the browser and re-measured. MIN 16->20, .dot { bottom: calc(20px + var(--row, 0) * 20px); }, strip.style.minHeight = `${92 + Math.max(0, rows.length - 1) * 20}px`, and .dot::after { top: -8px; right: -11px; bottom: -8px; left: -11px; }. After it: every mark's centre resolves to itself at 390, 768, 1280 and 1440 in both full and partial (elementFromPoint returns [0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8] everywhere); the audit target union measures 34x28 on every dot, so min(w,h) = 28 and the `< 28` floor still passes; closest-pair rises to 20.53px at 390, well over the behaviour gate's 12px; all marks still sit inside the strip. The guarantee is structural rather than data-dependent: MIN=20 makes same-row separation at least 20px against a 17px half-width, and the 14px half-height cannot reach a 20px row pitch. Two tightenings worth folding in. First, note that border-radius: 999px on a 34x28 box yields an ellipse, so the corners of that nominal rect are not tappable even though audit.mjs measures the rect - if you want the measured 28px to be the real 28px, set .dot::after { border-radius: 14px; } instead of 999px, which changes nothing visible (the pseudo is transparent) and makes the hit region a true stadium. Second, since the 28px floor is now met with exactly zero margin, add an explicit assertion to interaction-check.mjs rather than relying on audit.mjs: for every .dot, elementFromPoint at its own centre must resolve to itself, run at 390 and 1440. Without that, this class walks straight back in the next time the pitch or the expander is touched, because the existing closest-pair rule is structurally blind to occlusion.
confirmed.assertion: At every declared viewport, with touch set from the config, for every .dot: document.elementFromPoint(centreX, centreY).closest('.dot') === that dot. Assert it on full, partial, quiet and first-run.
confirmed.verdict: Confirmed by driving, not by reading. confirmed.element: a.kpi, .dot, .tab, .btn
confirmed.problem: The file contains no :active rule at all. Measured with the primary button actually held down: a.kpi, .dot and .tab all compute identically under hover and under press (transform, background, border, colour, ::before background all unchanged), and .btn's press is byte-identical to its hover. Separately, .dot — the surface's only genuinely interactive object — computes cursor: default, while a.kpi, .tab and .btn all compute pointer, so the nine marks give the pointer less acknowledgement than the cards that go nowhere.
confirmed.consequence: Under a coarse pointer there is no hover, so the press is the only channel by which the surface can confirm a touch registered — and it says nothing. Tapping a mark and tapping 2px beside it feel identical, which is exactly the ambiguity that makes a person tap a third and fourth time. On the desk, the marks never invite the pointer in the first place, so the reading that lives only in the tooltip stays undiscovered.
confirmed.fix: Keep two of the four, correct one, drop one, and fix the dot a different way. (1) cursor: pointer on .dot — the one uncontested line; it is a <button> and browsers give buttons cursor: default. (2) a.kpi:active { transform: translateY(0); } and nothing else — the press reads as the 2px lift being pushed back down, which is the whole gesture; leave border-color at hover's --line rather than jumping to solid --ink-4. (3) .btn:active { border-color: var(--ink-3); transform: translateY(1px); } — background already equals hover's --paper-3, so repeating it buys nothing; note .btn's transition list (line 359) omits transform, so the 1px is instant in both directions, which is correct for a press. (4) .dot: do NOT use transform on the pseudo. Either darken the token the disc already keys off — .dot:active { --disc: var(--ink-2); } (no cascade conflict; --disc is a background, not an animated property) — or, if a size change is wanted, use the independent transform property, .dot:active::before { scale: 0.9; }, which composes with the pop keyframes instead of losing to them (measured: computes scale:0.82 while transform stays identity). Even then, prove it on touch: with preventDefault on line 941 the :active state may never apply there, in which case the honest answer is that the dot's touch confirmation is the pinned tooltip, already shipped, and the press state is a desk-only refinement. (5) Drop .tab:active entirely, or set it to var(--ink) — --ink-2 inverts the hover ramp.
confirmed.assertion: For each of a.kpi, .dot, .tab and .btn: the computed style read with the primary pointer held down over the element differs from the computed style read on hover alone. And getComputedStyle(document.querySelector('.dot')).cursor === 'pointer'.

confirmed.element: .kpi.lead ("Open now / 9 / jobs not finished") on v=dark
confirmed.problem: `.kpi.lead` paints `background: var(--ink)`, and in the twin `--ink` is `#ffffff`. The denominator card therefore becomes a full white slab — the brightest object on the entire dark page by a wide margin, brighter than every numeral, and it sits in the middle of the KPI row. The file's own comment says the twin is "not an inversion: the grounds flip, the marks keep their jobs". This object's job did not survive the flip: in light it is the gravest, quietest plate in the row; in dark it is the loudest thing on screen.
confirmed.consequence: At night the eye is dragged to the one card in the row that carries no status and needs no attention, while the indigo meters — the marks that say what is actually slipping — lose the row entirely. The page's emphasis hierarchy inverts in the dark, which is the opposite of what the twin is for, and a bare white rectangle on a #0f0f10 ground is physically uncomfortable to look at in the room where a dark theme gets used.
confirmed.fix: Keep the inverted plate, take it off pure white. One rule, nothing else touched: `[data-v="dark"] .kpi.lead { background: var(--ink-2); border-color: var(--ink-2); }` -- #d4d4d8, Ink 5 in the eighteen. That cuts emitted luminance 34% (relative luminance 1.000 to 0.661) and removes the pure-white extreme, while the card stays unmistakably an inverted plate, so the protected shared-denominator reading survives intact. Crucially it needs no text changes and no new rules: the inherited `color: var(--paper)` #18181b lands at 11.98:1 on #d4d4d8, and the existing `.kpi.lead .t-small` at `--mark-ctx` #3f3f46 lands at 7.07:1 -- both comfortably AA, both already written. The light rule at line 277 is untouched, exactly as the seat asked. If the founder wants a deeper cut, `--ink-3` #a1a1aa is the next step down (64% luminance cut, label and numeral still 6.91:1) but it costs a second rule, because `.t-small` at #3f3f46 falls to 4.08:1 there and would have to move to `var(--paper-2)` #0f0f10 at 7.48:1 -- and a mid-grey plate starts to lose the authority the anchor card needs. Prefer `--ink-2`.
confirmed.assertion: With v=dark in states full, partial and quiet: the relative luminance of the computed background of `.kpi.lead` is lower than the relative luminance of the computed background of every other `.kpi` in the row, and its numeral still clears 4.5:1 against that background.
confirmed.verdict: problem affirmed, seat's fix replaced — The PROBLEM is real and reproduces; the PROPOSED FIX is wrong, so the finding is refuted with the fix corrected below. Confirmed against source and frames: lately.html:277 is `.kpi.lead { background: var(--ink); border-color: var(--ink); color: var(--paper); }` with no dark override anywhere (the only `[data-v="dark"]` rules are lines 92, 245, 317), and dark `--ink` is `#ffffff` (line 96) over a `--paper-2` ground of `#0f0f10`. In shots/dark-full--1440x960.png the denominator card is exactly what the seat describes: a ~285x230 pure-white slab, the largest bright region on the page by an order of magnitude, sitting in a row whose actual status marks are 3px indigo meters that read as nothing beside it. It is worse than the seat claims: at max-width 900px (line 438) `.kpi.lead` takes `grid-column: 1 / -1`, so at 390 and 768 the white plate is a full-width band across a near-black page, on the device most likely to be read at night. Class `defect` is correct and not overstated: nothing untrue is asserted and the product still does its job, but the row's emphasis visibly inverts after dark. Two corrections to the seat's framing: the light plate is not the 'quiet' object either -- pure black on #fafafa is also the highest-contrast object in that row, so this is not a contrast asymmetry but a luminance/halation one, which is why no gate catches it. Now the fix, which fails on two counts. (1) It breaks WCAG AA outright. `background: var(--paper-3)` gives a #27272a plate, but the fix never names the two rules that would survive it: `.kpi.lead` still carries `color: var(--paper)`, which in dark is #18181b, putting the OPEN NOW label and the 9 at 1.19:1 on that plate; and `.kpi.lead .t-small` (line 278) still pins 'jobs not finished' to `--mark-ctx` #3f3f46, which is 1.43:1. Both are hard failures the audit gate would reject on the next run. The fix gestures at 'numeral and label at var(--ink) and var(--ink-3)' but never says to unset the inherited `color`, and never mentions `.t-small` at all. (2) Its numbers, though correctly read off the source, are the wrong ones. #27272a against sibling cards at `--paper` #18181b is a 1.19:1 luminance step -- all but invisible -- so the denominator would stop reading as a categorically different object and become a marginally lighter sixth card, resting its whole identity on a #71717a hairline. The shared denominator is a protected object; the plate being a different KIND of surface is how a reader knows the 9 is the thing the other four are counted out of, not another status. Trading a glare problem for a weakened protected object is not an improvement at this bar.

confirmed.breaks: Low blast radius, but three things to re-check. (1) Re-run audit.mjs: the WCAG check composites against the real backdrop, and all three type roles on this card (t-label, t-num, t-small) change backdrop, so all three must be re-read even though the computed ratios above say they pass. (2) The card carries `box-shadow: 0 1px 2px var(--shadow)` where dark `--shadow` is rgba(15,15,16,0.6) -- a dark shadow under a light plate on a dark ground is invisible-to-muddy; check it does not read as a smear at the plate's lower edge, and drop it for this card in dark if it does. confirmed.element: .bar.part, and interaction-check.mjs's 'the unfinished week is hatched, open-topped and says so'
confirmed.problem: The protected treatment is that the current week is hatched and open-topped because the week is not over, and the source comment repeats it. The rule writes `border: 1px solid var(--accent); border-bottom: 0;` — it opens the bottom edge, which sits on the baseline and is invisible, and closes the top with a 1px solid indigo stroke plus `border-radius: 4px 4px 0 0`. Measured: borderTopWidth 1px rgb(79,70,229), borderLeftWidth 1px, borderRightWidth 1px, borderBottomWidth 0px. The column renders as a fully outlined capsule — the shape that says 'finished'. The behaviour gate certifies the opposite by measuring the wrong edge: `open: parseFloat(cs.borderBottomWidth) === 0` is true of a column with a closed top and would stay true if the top stroke were made heavier.
confirmed.consequence: The one shape cue that distinguishes an unfinished week from a finished one is not in the pixels; the hatch and the 'so far' callout carry the whole load. And the surface's own regression gate reports the contract as proven, so this cannot be caught by re-running it — it would have shipped as a certified pass.
confirmed.fix: Keep the seat's border rule but add the fade that its rationale actually asks for: `.bar.part { background: repeating-linear-gradient(135deg, var(--accent) 0 2px, rgba(17,17,17,0) 2px 6px); border: 0; border-left: 1px solid var(--accent); border-right: 1px solid var(--accent); border-radius: 0; -webkit-mask-image: linear-gradient(to top, #000 72%, transparent 100%); mask-image: linear-gradient(to top, #000 72%, transparent 100%); }` — I rendered this at 1440 and 390 and it reads as two verticals with the hatch dissolving upward, which is what 'open-topped' was meant to mean; the plain-cut version reads as a bounded container. `border-radius: 0` is correct here and should be kept: any top radius rounds the ends of the two rails and the hatch clip, which quietly re-caps the column. Then rewrite the gate to assert the edge that carries the meaning and to be non-vacuous — replace `open: parseFloat(cs.borderBottomWidth) === 0` with a conjunction of `parseFloat(cs.borderTopWidth) === 0`, `parseFloat(cs.borderTopLeftRadius) === 0 && parseFloat(cs.borderTopRightRadius) === 0`, and a check that the fade exists (`(cs.maskImage || cs.webkitMaskImage).includes('gradient')`), and keep the existing left/right rails asserted as non-zero so the fix cannot be undone by deleting the borders outright. Per L-05, write that assertion first and observe it red against the current master before landing the CSS; a green run on the unfixed file means the rewrite is as vacuous as the one it replaces.
confirmed.assertion: The current week's column computes borderTopWidth 0px, borderLeftWidth 1px and borderRightWidth 1px, and borderTopLeftRadius 0px, while every complete week's column computes a non-zero top radius and no border at all. Write the assertion against borderTopWidth first, observe it FAIL against the current build, then fix.
confirmed.verdict: Verified in the source and by driving the master in chromium at 1440 and 390. lately.html:239-244 is `.bar.part { background: repeating-linear-gradient(...); border: 1px solid var(--accent); border-bottom: 0; border-radius: 4px 4px 0 0; }`. Computed on the last column of ?v=light&state=full: borderTopWidth 1px solid rgb(79,70,229), borderLeftWidth 1px, borderRightWidth 1px, borderBottomWidth 0px, borderRadius 4px 4px 0px 0px. The seat's numbers are exact. The zero edge is the bottom, and the bar is bottom-anchored (.cols is align-items: flex-end, inset 0) so its bottom sits exactly on .baseline — removing that border removes nothing a reader can see. What is rendered is a fully outlined, top-rounded capsule: I clipped the last column and the top is a continuous indigo stroke with rounded corners, the same silhouette the finished bars carry. The protected object says the current week is 'hatched and open-topped', and the source's own comment two lines above says 'hatch plus an open top says "so far"'. The open top is not in the pixels; only the hatch and the '12 so far' label carry it. The second half is also correct and is the more valuable half: interaction-check.mjs:270 asserts `open: parseFloat(cs.borderBottomWidth) === 0`, which is true of a column with a closed top and would stay true if the top stroke were doubled. That is a vacuous assertion certifying its own opposite — lessons.md L-05/L-06, a class already paid for once, creeping back. This is not a restatement of what the gate proves; it is a demonstration that the gate proves nothing here. Severity: the seat's 'defect' is the right class and I am not raising it. The hatch and the 'so far' string are still present, so no reader is told an untrue thing (not misleading) and nothing fails to work (not blocking); one of three intended cues is visibly absent and contradicts the written contract, which is 'visibly wrong but passable'. The proposed fix is directionally right, constraint-safe and geometry-safe — I applied it live and re-measured: `* { box-sizing: border-box }` (lately.html:109) means dropping the top border changes nothing, the column stays 22px x 168px with the same top edge at both 1440 and 390, so .bar-val at `bottom: calc(var(--h) * 1% + 6px)` does not move; it introduces no hue (var(--accent) only) and 0 is on the radii ladder in elevate.config.json, so audit.mjs will not trip. confirmed.element: .gridline b, .record-tag, .bar-val and .xaxis — none is aria-hidden; .xaxis span.mute uses opacity: 0
confirmed.problem: The chart carries a written equivalent in `.sr` ('Twelve weeks of finished work … 27 Apr, 5; 4 May, 3; … 13 Jul, 12 so far. The best week before this one was 8.'), and every piece of visual furniture is left in the accessibility tree beside it. Walking the chart's non-aria-hidden leaves returns, in order: '6', '12', 'Best week · 8', '12 so far', then all twelve x-axis dates — of which eight compute `opacity: 0`, because `.xaxis span.mute` hides them visually with opacity rather than visibility, which removes them from sight but not from the tree.
confirmed.consequence: A screen-reader user hears the twelve weeks as a sentence and then hears the same chart again as a stream of loose numbers and dates, including eight dates that are not on the screen at all. The reading the sr line was written to give is buried in the duplicate.
confirmed.fix:
The seat's fix works but is more attributes than it needs and leaves one chart silent. Sharpen it three ways. (1) Instead of tagging .gridline, .record-tag and .bar-val separately, put aria-hidden="true" on the
wrapper in chart() — it already contains all three plus .baseline and .cols, holds no .sr, and one attribute stays correct as the plot gains children, whereas three named hooks rot. (2) Keep aria-hidden="true" on
as proposed. (3) Change .xaxis span.mute { opacity: 0 } to { visibility: hidden } as proposed — layout is identical, the flex box is preserved either way, and it is the right primitive for 'not there'; do it even though (2) already covers the tree, so no invisible element carries live text at all. Then the piece the seat missed: the first-run chart (lately.html ~line 779) is a second, separate literal — its own .plot with a .bar-val reading ' so far' and a one-tick .xaxis — and it has NO .sr line. Applying aria-hidden there, which any class-level pass will, would take that chart from partly spoken to entirely silent. Add a short sr equivalent beside it in the same commit:

This week so far: ${D.thisWeek} jobs finished, week commencing ${D.weeks[11].start}. Twelve weeks of history are not recorded yet.

. That keeps the protected drawn-but-empty plot and the partial-bucket treatment intact while making the state say in words what it draws.
confirmed.assertion: For every state that draws a chart, assert the accessible text of the `.chart` subtree is exactly the `.sr` sentence — no gridline value, record tag, bar callout or x-axis date appears outside it — and assert globally that no element with computed opacity 0 or width 0 contributes text to the accessibility tree.
confirmed.verdict: Verified in the code and in Chromium's own accessibility tree, not inferred. lately.html chart() emits .gridline b, .record-tag, .bar-val, twelve .xaxis spans and the .sr paragraph as siblings under .chart, and not one of them carries aria-hidden; the only aria-hidden in that subtree are the icon SVGs and .ghost-plot. Walking the chart's text leaves at 1440x960, state=full, returns exactly the sequence the seat names: '6', '12', 'Best week · 8', '12 so far', then all twelve dates, then the sr sentence. CDP Accessibility.getFullAXTree confirms the invisible ones are live: '4 MAY', '11 MAY', '25 MAY', '1 JUN', '15 JUN', '22 JUN' and '6 JUL' all come back ignored:false with no ignoredReasons, because .xaxis span.mute { opacity: 0 } (line 260) removes them from sight but not from the tree — the textbook opacity-versus-visibility mistake. So a screen-reader user does get the twelve weeks twice: once as the sentence the .sr line was written to give, and once as loose numerals plus seven dates that are not on the screen. Two corrections to the seat's write-up, neither of which changes the verdict. First, the count is seven, not eight: show = i % 3 === 0 || i === 11 leaves five ticks visible (27 Apr, 18 May, 8 Jun, 29 Jun, 13 Jul) and seven muted, which I counted in the DOM. Second, the consequence reverses the order — .sr is the last child of .chart, so the furniture is heard first and the sentence last, which makes the duplication worse, not better: the reader wades through the noise before reaching the line that explains it. Severity 'defect' is the right class and I am not raising it. Nothing here is untrue and nothing fails to work; the sentence is still correct and still reaches the reader. It is visibly — audibly — wrong and passable. Not covered by either gate: interaction-check.mjs asserts the chart HAS a spoken equivalent (words.chartSpoken) and that no .sr sits under aria-hidden, but never that the visual layer is kept out of the tree, and audit.mjs's visibility test at line 206 checks visibility and display only, so opacity:0 text is invisible to it too. confirmed.breaks: Low blast radius, but re-measure four things. (1) interaction-check.mjs reaches into this subtree three times — the gridline scale check (~line 254, querySelectorAll('.gridline') plus Number(textContent)), the partial-bucket check (~line 335, document.querySelector('.bar-val').textContent.includes('so far')), and the chartSpoken check (~line 326). All three are DOM queries, which aria-hidden does not affect, so all three should stay green; run the gate and confirm rather than assume. It is safe for the main chart because .sr is a sibling of .plot and .xaxis, not a descendant — but it WILL fire if the new first-run .sr from the sharpened fix is placed inside .plot or .xaxis instead of beside them, and it must be checked in the loading state too, where movementOne() is rendered inside <div class="sk-wrap" aria-hidden="true"> (line 805) and survives today only because line 957 strips .sk-wrap .sr; a new sr line must be caught by that same strip. confirmed.element: VIEW.empty, VIEW.error, VIEW.loading
confirmed.problem:
In the empty and error states, `
` contains no heading at all — the title is `

No work recorded yet

` and `

Tasks did not answer

`, styled at section rank but not marked as one, inside a `
` with no `aria-labelledby`. Measured: `main h1,h2,h3,h4` returns an empty list in both. Across all seven states, `[role=status], [aria-live], [role=alert]` returns zero elements. plan.html §07 specifies for the loading state 'a polite role="status" line'; what ships is `

Loading this reading.

` with no role, so it is inert text that is only found by walking to it.
confirmed.consequence: In the two states where something has gone wrong, a screen-reader user navigating by heading — the normal way to enter a page — finds 'Home' and then nothing, and no announcement ever tells them the reading failed or that it is being fetched. The error state is precisely the state where the reader most needs to be told what happened, and it is the state that says least.
confirmed.fix:
Keep the heading promotion exactly as proposed — `
` with `

No work recorded yet

`, and `mError` / 'Tasks did not answer' for the error state — but add `margin: 0` to the promoted headings rather than relying on a block-margin reset from a different finding landing first (see breaks: measured, the swap is NOT visually neutral on today's source). Change `role="status"` on the loading line exactly as proposed: `

Loading this reading.

` — that one matches plan.html §07 verbatim and needs no correction. Scope the alert more tightly than proposed: putting `role="alert"` on the error card's `.center` makes an implicitly atomic, assertive region out of a block that also contains the 'Try again' button and the 'Last good reading' timestamp, so the whole card — button label included — is read on any change inside it. Wrap only the title and the explanation instead, e.g. `
` around the `h2#mError` and its `p.t-body`, leaving the button and the timestamp outside the live region; the retry control stays reachable by heading and by tab, and a future retry-in-progress state cannot re-fire an assertive announcement of the entire card. Optional, and cheap while the file is open: the loading state has the same heading gap the seat found in the other two, because its only headings are inside `aria-hidden="true"` on `.sk-wrap` — the new `role="status"` line closes the announcement half but a heading-navigating reader still lands on nothing after 'Home'.

confirmed.element: .rail i — the four navigation glyphs at top left
confirmed.problem: The rail draws U+2302 ⌂, U+270E ✎, U+2611 ☑ and U+2197 ↗ with `font-family: Geist`. Geist does not carry the first three. Probed with `canvas.measureText` at 13px: ⌂ measures 7.8px under Geist, Geist Mono, serif and system-ui alike, ✎ measures 13px under all of them and ☑ 11.2px under all of them — identical widths meaning one fallback font is painting them in every case — while the control glyph "A" measures 8.68 under Geist against 9.39 serif and 8.39 system-ui, and ↗ measures 8.07 under Geist against 9.52 elsewhere, so Geist really does carry that one. Three of the four rail marks are therefore drawn by whatever the OS supplies. The audit's family check cannot see it: it reads computed `font-family`, which reports what the author wrote ("Geist"), not what the compositor painted.
confirmed.consequence: The first four objects at the top left of every frame at 768 and above are the only shapes on the surface not drawn by a face the studio chose, and they change between Windows, macOS and Linux — so the same screenshot is not the same product. On systems that resolve U+2611 to an emoji face it would also paint in colour, outside the eighteen.
confirmed.fix: Keep the direction - replace the four characters in shell()'s .rail markup with inline SVG in currentColor, aria-hidden, authored in ICON's stroke language - but fix the geometry. Draw on a 16x16 grid rendered at exactly 16px (`<svg width="16" height="16" viewBox="0 0 16 16">`), integer 1:1, which holds the 0.60 mark-to-tile ratio the 20px .glyph chips already establish (16/26 = 0.62). Hold stroke-width at 1.5 with stroke-linecap/linejoin round, identical to ICON.still/past/nobody/waiting, so the rail reads as the same pen rather than a scaled-up copy. Use `stroke="currentColor"` only - never ICON's hard-coded status hexes, which are reserved for the four status meanings and would import amber/red/indigo/emerald into inert furniture. currentColor is required, not optional, because .rail i.on inverts to color:var(--paper) on background:var(--ink). Then drop `font-size: 13px` from the .rail i rule: it no longer sets any type, and leaving a dead type declaration on a textless element is the kind of residue this lock exists to prevent. Redraw all four (including the arrow, which Geist does carry) so the set is one system, not three vectors beside one survivor.
confirmed.assertion: For every character rendered on the surface, the glyph is covered by Geist or Geist Mono — measured by comparing `canvas.measureText(ch)` under `13px Geist` and `13px "Geist Mono"` against `13px serif` and `13px monospace` and requiring at least one declared family to differ from every control family, not by reading computed `font-family`.
